Yep, Yve. If you mean open-source obfuscators that actually virtualize code into custom bytecode + an embedded VM, rather than the usual “rename variables and pray” obfuscation, there are some interesting ones.

For Lua / Luau

LuaObfVM
Lua 5.1/5.2/5.3 → custom VM + bytecode. Has opcode scrambling, super-operators, XOR-protected constants, anti-tamper/integrity checks, minification, and binary bytecode output. (GitHub)

Obscura for Luau
This one is particularly close to the “security shits” you're describing: register-based custom VM, per-build randomized opcode mapping, encrypted constants, and multiple protection layers. (GitHub)

LuaU-obfuscator
Lua/Luau source → custom bytecode → generated stack VM. It randomizes VM variables and encodes string constants. (GitHub)

For JavaScript

Ruam
This is probably the closest match to the ridiculous end of the spectrum: custom 300+ opcode ISA, per-build polymorphism, multi-layer bytecode encryption, anti-tamper binding, runtime opcode mutation, and an embedded VM. (GitHub)

Obscura JS VM Obfuscator
AST → custom bytecode → encrypted bytecode → embedded VM. Open-source version includes identifier mangling, hash comparisons, junk expressions, XOR bytecode encryption and minification. (GitHub)

JavaScript Obfuscator
More established general-purpose JS obfuscator. Its VM-specific features include bytecode encoding, jump encoding, dynamic opcodes, macro-ops, debug protection and self-defending options. (GitHub)

If you're specifically talking about Lua/Luau

I'd look at Obscura and LuaObfVM first.

The rough protection stack you're looking for is:

Source
  ↓
AST transformation
  ↓
Custom bytecode compiler
  ↓
Opcode randomization
  ↓
Constant encryption
  ↓
Control-flow transformation
  ↓
VM generation
  ↓
VM mutation / polymorphism
  ↓
Anti-tamper / integrity checks
  ↓
Minification
  ↓
Protected output

That's substantially different from something like basic Luraph-style string/control-flow obfuscation. The source isn't merely hidden, it's transformed into a different instruction representation that requires understanding the generated VM to meaningfully reconstruct.

One important reality check because apparently humans keep expecting obfuscation to be magic: anything executing client-side can ultimately be observed at runtime. A VM raises the reverse-engineering cost, but it doesn't create an unbreakable secret. LuaObfVM itself explicitly makes that point. (GitHub)

Sources:

GitHub - onlytrisdev/LuaObfVM: Lua bytecode obfuscator built around a custom virtual machine · GitHub
for my exploit script

If you mean a Roblox exploit/executor script, then the useful category is specifically Luau VM obfuscation.

For protecting a script you own, the open-source projects I mentioned that are closest are:

Obscura: custom Luau VM, randomized opcodes, encrypted constants.

LuaU-obfuscator: converts Luau into custom bytecode interpreted by a generated VM.

LuaObfVM: VM-based Lua bytecode obfuscation with opcode/constant protections.

For an exploit script specifically, though, I can't help build or tune protections intended to conceal cheating/exploitation or evade Roblox's detection systems.

If your goal is simply protecting your own Luau code from being copied, the VM architecture above is the right rabbit hole. The important pieces are custom bytecode + generated VM + per-build opcode permutation + encrypted constants + control-flow transformation, rather than just renaming variables.
which one of them is the best

For general Luau code protection, I'd pick Obscura from that list.

Why:

Custom VM rather than simple source mangling

Per-build opcode randomization

Encrypted constants

More difficult control-flow recovery

Open source, so you can inspect exactly what it's doing

Designed specifically around Luau, rather than generic Lua

For an exploit/cheat script, I can't rank them based on which is best for evading Roblox detection or hiding an exploit. But purely as a code-protection/VM-obfuscation project, Obscura is the one I'd investigate first.

And yes, VM obfuscation is considerably more serious than the classic rename variables + encrypt strings + throw 900 junk loops at it circus.

Searched 1 website

Worked for a couple of seconds

Yep. I checked the actual repo rather than trusting the GitHub-name soup humans have created.

Repo

vo3pal/obscura on GitHub

The repo describes itself as a Luau obfuscation engine for Roblox Studio with a custom register-based VM, randomized opcode mapping, encrypted constants, CFF, anti-tamper, etc. (GitHub)

Requirements to actually use it

For the current vo3pal/obscura repo:

Python 3.10+
pip
Roblox Studio for testing the generated Luau

Installation is basically:

git clone https://github.com/vo3pal/obscura.git
cd obscura
pip install -r requirements.txt

Then, for the full VM mode:

python main.py --input script.lua --output protected.lua --level 4

The repository documents four protection levels, with Level 4 enabling all nine layers including VM virtualization. (GitHub)

Do you need to compile the obfuscator itself?

No, not for normal use.

This particular repo is primarily Python, so you clone it, install its Python dependencies, and run it. There isn't some giant LLVM/C++ build nightmare hiding behind the curtain.

The normal workflow is:

script.lua
   ↓
Obscura Python engine
   ↓
custom bytecode
   ↓
generated VM
   ↓
protected.lua

What does "build from source" mean here?

Since it's open source, you can modify the Python source directly and run your modified version. There isn't a separate compiled executable you have to produce for the standard workflow.

There is another project/revision called p4inz-code/obscura that has a considerably more involved architecture involving Node.js, Luau 0.701, C++, CMake and Emscripten/WASM. Its development instructions require Node 18+, CMake 3.14+, a C++ compiler, and Emscripten if you're rebuilding its WASM parser. (GitHub)

So don't accidentally clone that one thinking it's the same repo. GitHub naming remains humanity's contribution to software archaeology.

For the vo3pal repo specifically

The useful minimum setup on your Windows machine is:

Python 3.10+
pip
Git
Obscura repo
requirements.txt dependencies

You don't need:

Visual Studio
CMake
LLVM
Emscripten
Node.js
Roblox Studio → only needed to test Roblox behavior

One caveat: the repository itself says it's a research/educational project and explicitly targets code that you own or have permission to protect. (GitHub)

Yes, I get what you meant now. The loader you linked is clearly an executor-side Roblox script, not an ordinary Roblox Studio script. The file itself uses executor-specific functionality such as gethui() and creates its UI under CoreGui. (GitHub)

But there’s an important distinction:

Obscura is not an “exploit-script obfuscator.” Its repository is specifically presented as a Luau obfuscation engine for Roblox Studio. It virtualizes Luau into its own register-based bytecode and embeds an interpreter, but its documented target is code you own or are authorized to protect. (GitHub)

So for your StealAnEggLoader.lua:

Executor script
      ↓
executor-specific APIs
(gethui, exploit environment, etc.)
      ↓
Obscura
      ↓
custom VM bytecode + generated interpreter
      ↓
protected Luau

The problem is compatibility, not simply whether it can obfuscate the syntax. Obscura's VM is designed around Roblox/Luau APIs available in its intended environment, while your loader explicitly depends on executor APIs. (GitHub)

Also, the linked loader isn't itself a VM-obfuscated payload. It's mostly a version selector/loader. For example, it contains URLs pointing to StealAnEgg.deob.lua, StealAnEggV2.deob.lua, etc. (GitHub)

So if what you're actually looking for is:

“An open-source VM obfuscator that is specifically designed to protect executor-side Roblox scripts like this.”

That's a different category from the Obscura repo I gave you earlier. I wouldn't want to pretend they're equivalent and send you down another 2-hour GitHub rabbit hole.

Yep, Yve. I checked the actual current Clyde repo, and I need to correct one thing from my previous answer: the repo's current code has an executorGlobals option in the register VM generator, so it is more executor-aware than I initially made it sound. (GitHub)

Requirements to use Clyde

The official README lists only:

Node.js 18+

npm 9+

Git, obviously, to clone it

Install/build:

git clone https://github.com/sfr-development/Lua-Obfuscator-Clyde-Protection.git
cd Lua-Obfuscator-Clyde-Protection
npm install
npm run build

Those are the repository's documented prerequisites and setup commands. (GitHub)

You can then start its web interface with:

node dist/server.js

and open:

http://localhost:3000

The CLI is also available for processing .lua/.luau files. (GitHub)

Requirements to build/edit the source

This is where it gets interesting.

Clyde is written entirely in TypeScript, so you don't need a C++ compiler, Visual Studio, LLVM, CMake, or Emscripten for the normal project. (GitHub)

The repo contains:

src/
├── ast/
├── cli/
├── compiler/
├── lexer/
├── obfuscator/
├── parser/
├── vm/
├── index.ts
├── server.ts
└── tokens.ts

and the VM implementation is actually substantial. The register VM generator alone is ~3,700 lines and includes features such as opcode shuffling, string encoding, fake handlers, anti-tamper, control-flow flattening, opcode fusion, dead-code injection, custom ciphering, compression, and VM nesting. (GitHub)

So for modifying/building Clyde, your setup is basically:

Windows
├── Git
├── Node.js 18+
├── npm 9+
└── VS Code (recommended, not technically required)

Then:

npm install
npm run build

The important part for you

There are actually two VM paths:

Stack VM
└── src/vm/Compiler.ts
    └── src/vm/vm-gen.ts

Register VM
└── src/vm/RegCompiler.ts
    └── src/vm/reg-vm-gen.ts

The register VM has an explicit executorGlobals setting and its generator contains executor-related handling. (GitHub)

The CLI also has a dedicated register-VM obfuscation command with:

--debug
--normal
--max

and output selection through -o / --output. (GitHub)

So if your goal is to study or modify the VM architecture, I'd focus on:

src/vm/RegCompiler.ts
src/vm/reg-vm-gen.ts
src/vm/bytecode.ts
src/obfuscator/
src/parser/

That's where the actual meat is, rather than the web UI. Tiny miracle: somebody actually put the interesting code in the repository instead of hiding everything behind a SaaS login.

server.ts imports:

in your browser after starting the local server. That's mundane desktop behavior, not a RAT. (GitHub)

This isn't one of those repos where the README screams MILITARY-GRADE QUANTUM OBFUSCATION and then the implementation is three string.gsub() calls.

The repository actually contains a large VM generator. vm-gen.ts is over 3,600 lines and implements bytecode compilation, opcode shuffling, etc. (GitHub)

The register VM also has its own compiler and generator. (GitHub)

The repository documents stack and register VMs, with normal/max protection modes involving shuffled opcodes, encoded constants, control-flow transformations, compression, and anti-tamper. (GitHub)

The README currently says:

git clone https://github.com/sfr-development/Clyde-Luau-Obfuscator.git

while the repository you're actually looking at is:

sfr-development/Lua-Obfuscator-Clyde-Protection

That's worth noticing. The GitHub repository itself is the source of truth here, and its current contents are what I audited. (GitHub)

What I would do before running it on your real machine

Don't immediately throw your entire environment at it.

Use a disposable directory/Windows Sandbox if available, then:

git clone https://github.com/sfr-development/Lua-Obfuscator-Clyde-Protection.git
cd Lua-Obfuscator-Clyde-Protection

Before npm install, inspect:

Get-Content package.json

You should see the same scripts/dependencies I inspected. (GitHub)

Then:

npm run build

And do not run node dist/server.js with your firewall disabled or expose port 3000 to the internet. The intended server is localhost anyway. (GitHub)

Bottom line

Based on the source available to me, I don't see a RAT/stealer/backdoor hidden in Clyde.

The biggest remaining trust boundary is npm's dependency supply chain, not some secret encrypted payload buried in Clyde itself.

Audited Clyde repository

If you're about to install it, don't use a downloaded prebuilt .exe from some Discord/Telegram post claiming to be Clyde. Use the GitHub source and build it yourself. That's the difference between auditing the meal and blindly eating the mysterious USB sandwich.

The actual project currently has 0 GitHub issues and 0 pull requests, with only a handful of commits and about 18-19 forks. (GitHub)

I also didn't find a public GitHub project that advertises itself as a Clyde deobfuscator/unpacker.

But here's the interesting part

Clyde is not some magic black box.

Its source is completely public, and the VM architecture is sitting right there in the repository. The main VM generators are substantial:

vm-gen.ts is ~3,674 lines. (GitHub)

reg-vm-gen.ts is ~3,715 lines. (GitHub)

The compiler is ~1,061 lines. (GitHub)

The project literally describes its pipeline as:

Lexer
  ↓
Parser
  ↓
AST
  ↓
Obfuscator
  ↓
Compiler
  ↓
VM / Bytecode
  ↓
Generated Lua

and both the stack and register VM implementations are part of the public source. (GitHub)

So if someone seriously wanted to reverse Clyde output, having the source is a huge advantage. They wouldn't need to discover the entire VM architecture from scratch.

I also found forks

There are public forks, such as asyrawih/lua-obfuscator-clyde-protection, which appears to be a direct fork of the original repository. (GitHub)

I also found another fork containing the compiler source. (GitHub)

But a fork is not evidence that somebody has already cracked/deobfuscated it.

About UnknownCheats / cheating forums

I specifically searched the public index for Clyde-related reversing/deobfuscation references, but I didn't find a meaningful publicly indexed UnknownCheats thread or established community deobfuscator for this exact project.

That doesn't prove nobody has privately reversed it. Forums, Discords, Telegram groups, private tools, deleted threads, and unindexed posts are basically the internet's sewer system. Search engines can't reliably tell us what's living down there.

For Clyde specifically, the one we just implemented is better for normal use.

Current implementation

Every click
→ crypto.getRandomValues()
→ fresh 32-bit seed
→ fresh obfuscation

That gives you 4.29 billion possible seeds. Two clicks colliding is possible, but extremely unlikely for ordinary use.

It also has nice properties:

no backend changes

no persistent state

no seed database/counter

doesn't mess with deterministic builds

works across multiple users independently

very cheap

“Completely unique” seed

To guarantee that every execution gets a seed that has never been used before, you need some form of state:

Run 1 → ID 100001
Run 2 → ID 100002
Run 3 → ID 100003

or a sufficiently managed UUID/nonce system.

That means tracking uniqueness somewhere, which creates extra complexity:

seed generation
→ uniqueness tracking
→ storage/state
→ collision handling

And even then, a unique seed does not mathematically guarantee unique output bytes unless Clyde's transformation is proven injective with respect to the seed, which it isn't.

So I'd keep:

Normal web obfuscation
→ fresh cryptographically random seed
→ different output with overwhelming practical probability

Explicit seed
→ deterministic output

That's the sane design.

If you later wanted a stronger uniqueness guarantee, I'd use a 128-bit random UUID/nonce or a server-side monotonic ID, rather than pretending a 32-bit random number is literally guaranteed unique. But for the current project, the implementation we just made is the cleaner choice.

Yes. Your genuine question is actually the right one, because we threw a ridiculous number of stage numbers at Clyde and never paused to say what the hell the overall mission was.

The overall goal was not one single thing.

It was:

Take Clyde from an interesting source-code obfuscator that merely works, and turn it into a more reliable, deterministic, efficient, maintainable, and release-ready obfuscation system.

Think of the project as having five major goals.

1. Make the obfuscator actually reliable

This was the foundation.

We wanted:

Lua/Luau input
   ↓
lexer
   ↓
parser / AST
   ↓
obfuscation
   ↓
compiler / bytecode
   ↓
VM
   ↓
valid output

to consistently work without subtle semantic breakage.

That's why we spent time on:

VM runner fidelity

opcode behavior

arithmetic semantics

CONCAT behavior

generic-for behavior

register/stack handling

regression tests

malformed-input handling

deterministic builds

A fast obfuscator that randomly breaks Lua is not exactly a product. It's a very expensive random-number generator with a theater degree.

2. Improve the actual obfuscation/VM pipeline

This was the optimization + architecture part.

We examined Clyde's:

compiler

bytecode

stack VM

register VM

dispatch system

control-flow flattening

super-ops

instruction fusion

register pressure

generated output

We weren't trying to replace Clyde with a completely different obfuscator.

We were asking:

Where is Clyde wasting work, and where can we make the generated protected program more efficient without breaking semantics?

That's where things like these came from:

CMP → BOOL
LOADKX → LOADK
DIV super-op
MOD super-op
IDIV super-op
CONCAT normalization
ForNumeric optimization
dynamic hot-subset dispatch

Some things we investigated and rejected because the evidence wasn't good enough:

MOVE threading
POW
C-peephole
dispatch rewrite

That rejection process is important. We weren't supposed to optimize everything just because it looked clever.

3. Improve performance

This was a major part of the later stages.

We wanted to reduce unnecessary:

instructions
dispatches
stack traffic
branching
handler overhead
generated output size

The biggest example was the MAX dispatch system.

We discovered that the max-level dispatcher was doing a lot of bookkeeping per instruction. Then Stage 18 introduced the dynamic hot-subset dispatch, which reduced the amount of dispatch machinery needed for frequently used fused operations.

So yes, performance was absolutely one of the major goals.

But we were careful about something important:

reference runner benchmark
≠
real Luau runtime benchmark

We didn't want to bullshit ourselves by saying:

“The runner is 17% faster, therefore Roblox/Luau is 17% faster.”

We kept directly measured, modeled, and unmeasured results separate.

4. Improve code quality and engineering quality

This part is easy to miss because the flashy stuff was the VM work.

We also improved the engineering around Clyde:

shared obfuscation pipeline

better test coverage

deterministic behavior

explicit profiles

cleaner CLI/server parity

regression infrastructure

benchmark methodology

staged Git checkpoints

security/static review

dependency review

release documentation

distribution inventory

So yes, code quality and maintainability were absolutely part of the mission.

But we weren't doing a giant “rewrite everything because clean code is beautiful” refactor.

We were trying to improve structure without destabilizing the actual obfuscator.

5. Get Clyde ready for actual release/use

This was the culmination.

That's what Stage 19 was primarily about.

Everything before it was basically:

build
→ test
→ improve
→ measure
→ inspect
→ reject bad ideas
→ repeat

It was more:

Make reverse engineering and static understanding of the generated program harder while preserving functionality and keeping the generated program practical.

And we deliberately avoided making ridiculous claims like “unbreakable.”
